sentences.text: Fragmentary remains suggest that adult Liliensternus could have reached lengths of 7 to 9 meters.
Liliensternus was approximately 5.15 meters long and may have weighed about 127 kilograms.
In Liliensternus, the tibia is 409 mm long and the femur is 440 mm long.
Liliensternus had an unusually short ilium, similar to the condition seen in Dilophosaurus.
Liliensternus is the best-represented Triassic theropod from Europe and one of the largest known.
Liliensternus had five fingers with smaller fourth and fifth digits, representing a possible transitional stage between five-fingered Triassic theropods and three-fingered Jurassic theropods.
The type specimens of Liliensternus were discovered near Großer Gleichberg in Thuringia, Germany.
Count Hugo Rühle von Lilienstern discovered the type specimens in the winter of 1932/1933.
Friedrich von Huene described Liliensternus in 1934.

The syntypes of Liliensternus were discovered by Count Hugo Rühle von Lilienstern in the winter of 1932–1933 in marl deposits from the Late Triassic Norian stage, approximately 228 to 208 million years ago.
In 1993, Gilles Cuny and Peter Galton described a new species assigned to this genus, Liliensternus airelensis.
Liliensternus was an active bipedal carnivore that likely preyed on large herbivores like Plateosaurus.
Liliensternus is classified as a basal member of the Neotheropoda.
Rowe discovered in 1989 that Liliensternus is more derived than Dilophosaurus.
Originally assigned to Halticosauridae, Liliensternus is now considered a basal member of Neotheropoda.
Liliensternus lived during the Norian to Rhaetian stages, from 227.3 to 201.4 million years ago.
It is debated whether Liliensternus airelensis should remain in Liliensternus or be assigned to the separate genus Lophostropheus.
In 2007, Martin Ezcurra and Cuny reassigned the material of L. airelensis to their own genus, Lophostropheus.
